definitions.definition: The darśana that enumerates the twenty-five principles in order to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti; its knowledge is the discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2) that removes the threefold suffering.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Each of the twenty-five principles: mūlaprakṛti, mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities, the five subtle elements, the five gross elements, and puruṣa (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61). Knowledge of them liberates.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: The conscious principle: neither producer nor product (SK 3); the opposite of the manifest and the unmanifest in being without guṇas, discriminating, subject, individual and conscious (SK 11); witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent (SK 19); many (SK 18). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, etc. (SK 17). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Both name the conscious self; Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is plural, inactive and without properties, whereas Advaita's ātman is one (with Brahman) and Nyāya's ātman bears qualities.

literal: that which brings forth; nature, source

definitions.definition: The unconscious, productive principle consisting of the three guṇas in equilibrium (SS 1.61), from which mahat and the other principles emerge (SK 22); one and common to all puruṣas (SK 11); inferred from its effects (SK 8, 15–16); it acts for puruṣa's experience and liberation and binds and releases itself (SK 57–63). In SK 3 'prakṛti' also names any principle that produces another (the seven prakṛti-vikṛtis).

cross_language.note: also renders svabhāva; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
also renders svabhāva; as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Gauḍapāda lists māyā among the synonyms of prakṛti (on SK 22) and Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.10 equates them, but Sāṃkhya holds prakṛti real and independent, while Advaita holds māyā indeterminable and not a second reality.

definitions.definition: Prakṛti as the uncaused root of all modifications, itself not a modification (SK 3); 'the rootless root' (SS 1.67).
Synonym of prakṛti as the principal cause of the world (SK 11, 57); the term under which Vedānta and other critics discuss the Sāṃkhya cause.

cross_language.note: as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Prakṛti in its unmanifest state: uncaused, eternal, pervasive, inactive, one, unsupported, non-merging, partless and independent — the opposite of the manifest (SK 10) — and known through its effects (SK 8, 14–16).

The evolutes of prakṛti, from mahat to the gross elements: caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, supported, merging, composite and dependent (SK 10), consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminating, object, common, unconscious and productive (SK 11).
Puruṣa as knower, the third member of 'the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower' whose discriminating knowledge is the better means (SK 2).
A principle that is a product only and produces no further principle: the sixteen (manas, ten capacities, five gross elements) (SK 3; Tattvasamāsa 2).

The first evolute of prakṛti (SK 22), identical with buddhi; Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms buddhi, āsurī, mati, khyāti, jñāna, prajñā. Vijñānabhikṣu salutes mahat as the self-born Lord, sprout of the world.

The determining faculty (adhyavasāya, SK 23), whose sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power and whose tāmasa form is their opposite; the door-keeper among the instruments (SK 35), which accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37).

The evolute of mahat whose nature is self-assertion (abhimāna); from it proceed the eleven organs (from its vaikṛta, sāttvika form) and the five subtle elements (from its bhūtādi, tāmasa form), both with its taijasa form (SK 24–25). It, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

cross_language.note: also renders asmimāna; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: The eleventh organ, partaking of both the sense and action capacities, whose function is constructive thought (saṅkalpa) (SK 27); one of the three internal instruments (SK 33).
The eleven capacities produced from ahaṃkāra: five sense capacities, five action capacities and manas (SK 24–27); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).
Ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose (SK 26), whose function is mere awareness (ālocana) of sound and the rest (SK 28); later called jñānendriya.
Speech, hands, feet, anus and genitals (SK 26), whose functions are speaking, grasping, walking, excreting and delight (SK 28).
The five non-specific (aviśeṣa) elements — of sound, touch, form, taste and smell — produced from ahaṃkāra as bhūtādi (SK 25, 38), from which the five gross elements arise (SK 22).

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Space, air, fire, water and earth, produced from the five subtle elements (SK 22; Gauḍapāda on SK 22); specific (viśeṣa), and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 38).

The three constituents of prakṛti — sattva, rajas, tamas — of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, serving illumination, activity and restraint, and functioning by mutual domination, support, production and pairing (SK 12).

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: The guṇa that is light and illuminating (SK 13), of the nature of pleasure (SK 12); predominant in the upper worlds (SK 54). Vācaspati also uses 'sattva' for buddhi.
The guṇa that is stimulating and mobile (SK 13), of the nature of pain (SK 12); predominant in the middle world (SK 54); suffering is a modification of rajas (Vācaspati).

(1) The guṇa that is heavy and enveloping (SK 13), of the nature of delusion (SK 12), predominant at the root of creation (SK 54). (2) The first of the five kinds of error (viparyaya), eightfold (SK 48): taking the eight non-selves (prakṛti, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, the five subtle elements) for the self (Kramadīpikā; Gauḍapāda).
The three guṇas taken together, of which prakṛti and the manifest consist (SK 14; Tattvasamāsa 4).
Prakṛti defined as the equilibrium of sattva, rajas and tamas (SS 1.61); creation proceeds from their inequality.

literal: doctrine that the effect is existent

definitions.definition: The doctrine that the effect exists in its material cause before its production, argued with five reasons (SK 9; SS 1.114–118); production is manifestation and destruction is dissolution into the cause (SS 1.121).

literal: doctrine that the effect is non-existent (before production)

definitions.definition: The rival (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) view that the effect is new, rejected by Sāṃkhya: the non-existent cannot be produced, like a man's horn (SK 9; SS 1.114).
Real transformation: prakṛti operates through the guṇas by combination and transformation, like water taking on different tastes in different receptacles (SK 16).
Production understood as the manifestation of what already exists, as a pot is manifested by a lamp (SS 5.59; cf. 1.120).
The three characters of the specific (gross) elements, according to the predominance of sattva, rajas or tamas (SK 38).
The five subtle elements, which lack the calm, turbulent and dull differentiation (SK 38).
The gross elements (SK 38); the specifics are threefold: subtle bodies, bodies born of parents, and gross elements (SK 39).
Ahaṃkāra in its sāttvika aspect, from which the eleven organs proceed (SK 25).
Ahaṃkāra in its rājasa aspect, from which both groups (organs and subtle elements) proceed (SK 25).
Ahaṃkāra in its tāmasa aspect, from which the subtle elements proceed (SK 25).
The emergence of the principles from the unmanifest in order (Tattvasamāsa 5; SK 22).
Dissolution of the principles into their causes in reverse order, the unmanifest itself not dissolving (Tattvasamāsa 6 and commentaries).
(1) The manifest, as that which 'merges' into its cause (SK 10). (2) The subtle body that transmigrates (SK 20, 40–42). (3) The inferential mark (SK 5).

The subtle body produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements, which transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, and plays its parts like an actor (SK 40–42); it cannot stand without a support (SK 41).

equivalents.note: Within Sāṃkhya the 'subtle' (sūkṣma) bodies of SK 39 are the liṅga of SK 40; Vedānta's sūkṣma-śarīra is composed differently.

definitions.definition: The subtle bodies, constant, as against the perishing bodies born of mother and father (SK 39); denied by Vindhyavāsin (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).
The gross body, which perishes (SK 39); in the Kramadīpikā made of six sheaths — hair, blood and flesh from the mother, sinew, bone and marrow from the father.
The thirteenfold instrument — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the ten capacities — which seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32); it acts only for puruṣa's purpose (SK 31).
Buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, the threefold internal instrument operating in all three times; the door-keeper, of which the ten external instruments are the doors (SK 33, 35).
The ten capacities, operating in the present and presenting objects to the three internal ones (SK 33).
The function of the sense capacities: mere awareness of sound and the rest (SK 28).
The function of manas (SK 27).
The nature of ahaṃkāra (SK 24); also the misidentification by which puruṣa seems colored (SS 6.28).
The nature of buddhi (SK 23); perception is determination concerning each object (SK 5), explained by Vācaspati as a predominance of sattva in buddhi.
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at mouth and nose.
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the navel.
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the heart.
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the throat.
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the joints.

The eight dispositions of buddhi — virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power and their opposites (SK 23) — innate, natural or acquired (SK 43), which perfume the subtle body (SK 40) and by seven of which prakṛti binds herself (SK 63).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) leading to upward movement (SK 44), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda defines it by compassion, giving and the yamas and niyamas of the Pātañjala. With knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to act as causes (SK 67).
The tāmasa opposite of virtue (SK 23), leading to downward movement (SK 44).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); through knowledge comes liberation (SK 44); in its highest form the complete, pure, single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64). Gauḍapāda distinguishes external (scriptural) from internal knowledge (of prakṛti and puruṣa), only the latter liberating.
The tāmasa opposite of knowledge (SK 23); from it (viparyaya) comes bondage (SK 44).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); by itself it leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda distinguishes external dispassion (from seeing the faults of objects) and internal (seeing even pradhāna as like a dream). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra makes it a support of meditation (3.36).
The tāmasa opposite of dispassion; from passion of the nature of rajas comes saṃsāra (SK 45); meditation is its removal (SS 3.30); it is not quieted by enjoyment (SS 4.27).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentaries list eight powers — becoming minute (aṇimā), great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going wherever one wishes. In Sāṃkhya these powers are aiśvarya, not 'siddhi'; attachment to them is the error called moha.
The tāmasa opposite of power (SK 23), bringing obstruction (SK 45).

The three origins of the dispositions (SK 43): innate, as in Kapila at the first creation; natural, as in Brahmā's sons at sixteen or in Āsuri through contact with the supreme sage; acquired, as in ordinary people, with a teacher as occasioning cause.
The first embryonic stage; the stages beginning with kalala rest on the body, as the dispositions rest on buddhi (SK 43).

The intellectual creation of fifty kinds — five errors, twenty-eight incapacities, nine contentments, eight accomplishments — arising from the inequality of the guṇas (SK 46–51); with the liṅga creation it forms the twofold creation (SK 52).

(1) The opposite of knowledge, from which bondage comes (SK 44). (2) The first class of the creation of cognitions, fivefold — darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom — with sixty-two subdivisions (SK 47–48); the Tattvasamāsa calls it 'five-jointed avidyā'.

equivalents.note: The five errors are identified with the five afflictions (avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa, abhiniveśa) by the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.8 ('these same, by their own names, are darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom'), and implied by the Tattvasamāsa's 'five-jointed avidyā'.

definitions.definition: In the Tattvasamāsa, the five-jointed avidyā = the five errors (Tattvasamāsa 12; Kramadīpikā). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra denies that bondage is caused by an avidyā that is unreal (SS 1.20–26) or that avidyā is the world's material cause (SS 5.65).
The second error, eightfold (SK 48): attachment to or self-assertion for the eight powers, through which even gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).
The third error, tenfold: attachment to the five objects, divine and human (SK 48; Gauḍapāda).
The fourth error, eighteenfold: aversion or resentment concerning the eight powers and ten objects (SK 48; commentaries).
The fifth error, eighteenfold: the despair of one who dies amid, or falls from, the powers and objects (SK 48; Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).

The twenty-eight incapacities: injuries of the eleven organs (deafness, blindness, numbness, etc.) and seventeen injuries of buddhi, the reversals of the nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 49).

Nine contentments (SK 50): four internal — resting content with nature, with outward means (such as the triple staff and water-pot), with time, or with luck — and five external, from abstaining from objects for seeing their faults; they do not bring liberation and, with error and incapacity, are the curb on accomplishment (SK 51).

In the Sāṃkhya Kārikā, the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge: reasoning, words (hearing), study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving (SK 51) — not supernormal powers, which Sāṃkhya calls aiśvarya (SK 23).
The accomplishment of reflecting on 'what is true, what is highest, what is the final good' until the difference of puruṣa and pradhāna is known (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).

(1) The subtle element of sound and the quality of space (SK 22, 28). (2) The accomplishment of knowledge arising from hearing words of instruction (SK 51). (3) In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, verbal testimony = reliable instruction (SS 1.101); sound is not eternal and not sphoṭa (SS 5.57–58).
The accomplishment of gaining knowledge of the twenty-five principles by studying texts (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
The accomplishment of receiving knowledge from a friend who has it (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).

The accomplishment of receiving knowledge from the venerable after serving them with shelter, medicine, staff, water-pot, food and clothing (Gauḍapāda on SK 51); Vācaspati is recalled as deriving it from the root 'dai' (to purify), the purity of discriminative knowledge (low confidence).
The three kinds of suffering that prompt the inquiry (SK 1): internal, from other beings, and from the divine (named by the commentaries); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1).
Internal suffering, bodily (from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm) and mental (from desire, anger, separation from the dear, etc.) (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati on SK 1).
Suffering caused by humans, animals, birds, reptiles, insects and plants (commentaries on SK 1).
Suffering from supernatural or cosmic agencies: cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning (Gauḍapāda) or possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas and planets (Vācaspati).
The inquiry into the means of destroying the three sufferings, prompted by being struck by them (SK 1).

literal: known from what is heard (the Veda)

definitions.definition: The Vedic ritual means, which are like the seen means because impure, perishable and graded (SK 2).
The two qualities seen means lack (SK 1) and final isolation has (SK 68): certain (invariable) and final (without recurrence).
Final, without recurrence — of the cessation of suffering in kaivalya (SK 1, 68).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and reliable testimony — since all others are included in them (SK 4); Vācaspati reduces postulation, absence, inclusion and tradition to these.
Perception, defined as determination concerning each object (SK 5); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, the cognition that, in contact, reflects its object's form (SS 1.89).
Threefold inference preceded by knowledge of the mark and the marked (SK 5); by inference from general correlation supersensible things (prakṛti, puruṣa) are known (SK 6).

Reliable testimony (reliable revelation, SK 5), establishing what neither perception nor inference establishes (SK 6); the reliable person is devoted to his work, free of passion and aversion, knowing and virtuous (Kramadīpikā).
Inference whose object's class has been seen before (e.g., fire from smoke); with śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa one of the three kinds (commentaries on SK 5).
Inference by exclusion (= avīta) (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Inference from general correlation, by which things beyond the senses are known (SK 6), such as the senses as instruments (Vācaspati), and both prakṛti and puruṣa (SS 1.103).
Inference proceeding by agreement, establishing its object; divided into pūrvavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Inference proceeding by difference, negating (the alternatives) — the śeṣavat kind (Vācaspati on SK 5).

Discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2), which buddhi accomplishes (SK 37); it is accomplished through practice of the principles, renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

The discernment of the distinctness of puruṣa and prakṛti (sattva), culminating in the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64); called the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (Vācaspati).

notes: The compound is standard in Yoga (YS 2.26); the SK uses vijñāna/jñāna, Pañcaśikha 'khyāti'.

definitions.definition: The failure to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti, the cause of their conjunction and so of bondage (SS 1.55); beginningless, removed by discrimination like darkness by light; bondage is non-discrimination alone (SS 6.12–16). The manifest and unmanifest are 'non-discriminating' (SK 11).

(1) Puruṣa's intrinsic isolation (SK 19). (2) The goal: isolation that is certain and final, attained when the body falls and pradhāna, its purpose fulfilled, ceases (SK 68); prakṛti's activity is for its sake (SK 17, 21).
Liberation, which comes through knowledge (SK 44); defined in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as the indifference of one of the two (SS 3.66).

In Sāṃkhya, release belongs to prakṛti, not puruṣa (SK 62); it is threefold in the Tattvasamāsa commentaries — by increase of knowledge, calming of passion, and total exhaustion of virtue and non-virtue (Kramadīpikā); it is not the manifestation of bliss (SS 5.74).

Bondage comes from error (SK 44) and belongs to prakṛti, which binds herself by seven forms (SK 62–63); it is threefold — to prakṛti, to the modifications, and through gifts (Tattvasamāsa and Kramadīpikā).

The result of dispassion (without discrimination) (SK 45): a dissolution into prakṛti or its evolutes, taken for liberation, from which one rises again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'.

The state of one who, after perfect knowledge, remains embodied through the momentum of impressions like a potter's wheel (SK 67); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the 'one liberated while living' and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers (SS 3.78–84).

notes: The SK itself does not use the word.

definitions.definition: Impressions whose momentum keeps the knower embodied after knowledge (SK 67; SS 3.84), exhausted at the fall of the body (Gauḍapāda).
The image for the knower's continued embodiment by residual momentum (SK 67; SS 3.83).

The repeated contemplation of the principles from which the liberating knowledge arises (SK 64); described by Vācaspati as long, reverent, uninterrupted meditative cultivation after hearing and reasoning, and by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

equivalents.note: Vācaspati's description of tattvābhyāsa (long, reverent, uninterrupted) echoes Yoga's definition of firm practice (YS 1.14); Sāṃkhya's practice has the principles as its content.

definitions.definition: In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, the form of the practice of the principles: discrimination comes by giving up (each principle) with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).
Practice, with dispassion a support of meditation (SS 3.36) and of the cessation of coloring (SS 6.29).
Meditation is the removal of passion, accomplished through the cessation of mental modifications (SS 3.30–31); meditation is mind without object (SS 6.25).
Posture is what is steady and pleasant (SS 3.34); there is no fixed rule (SS 6.24).
Torpor in meditation, from which one must turn away, 'say the teachers' (SS 6.30).
Distraction in meditation, from which one must turn away (SS 6.30).
Puruṣa is witness (SK 19), by direct relation (SS 1.161); the witness of deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148).
Puruṣa as seer (SK 19), who sees prakṛti like a spectator once knowledge arises (SK 65).
Puruṣa is non-agent (SK 19); agency belongs to the guṇas and puruṣa only appears as agent (SK 20); ahaṃkāra is the agent (SS 6.54).
Puruṣa's neutrality (SK 19).
Puruṣa, indifferent, which appears as agent through conjunction (SK 20); on knowledge it is the indifferent onlooker (SK 66).
Puruṣa as experiencer, one proof of its existence (SK 17); experience culminates in consciousness (SS 1.104).
Experience, which buddhi accomplishes for puruṣa (SK 37); with liberation, one of the two purposes for which prakṛti acts (commentaries on SK 21).

The purpose — experience and liberation — for which the instruments act (SK 31, 36), the liṅga plays its parts (SK 42) and prakṛti creates (SK 56); the supreme puruṣārtha is the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1).
That aggregates exist for another's sake, proving puruṣa (SK 17); prakṛti's undertaking is for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60).

The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti, like that of the lame and the blind, from which creation proceeds (SK 21) and the unconscious appears conscious (SK 20); due to non-discrimination (SS 1.55); though it remains after knowledge, there is no motive for creation (SK 66).
The simile for the conjunction of puruṣa (who sees but cannot move) and prakṛti (who moves but cannot see) (SK 21).
The need for a controller, a proof of puruṣa (SK 17); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
The apparent coloring of puruṣa by buddhi's modifications, through which agency seems to belong to it (SS 1.164); not real coloring like the red flower's on a crystal but misidentification (SS 6.28).
Puruṣa, reflected in buddhi and taking on its shade, appears to have knowledge and pleasure, while buddhi, taking on the shade of consciousness, appears conscious (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Vācaspati's name for puruṣa as consciousness, to which suffering is disagreeable (on SK 1, 5).
Puruṣa is conscious; the manifest and unmanifest are unconscious (acetana) (SK 11); the unconscious liṅga appears conscious through conjunction (SK 20).

Classical Sāṃkhya recognizes no established Īśvara as creator: Gauḍapāda argues the attributeless could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds 'Īśvara is not established' (1.92–99; 5.2–12; 6.64), yet admits emergent lords — the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Theistic Sāṃkhya (Vijñānabhikṣu) salutes the Lord.
The whole doctrine that the SK condenses (SK 72): ten fundamental topics and the fifty categories of the creation of cognitions (Yuktidīpikā, Māṭhara, Kramadīpikā); also the name of a lost work.

The ten fundamental topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra: pradhāna's existence, oneness and purposiveness; puruṣa's distinctness; being for another; plurality of puruṣas; separation; conjunction; the remaining function (persistence of the body); non-agency (lists differ slightly in order).
Kapila, by whom the secret knowledge was expounded (SK 69; Gauḍapāda).
Kapila as the first knower who, assuming a created mind, taught the doctrine to Āsuri out of compassion (saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.25, ascribed to Pañcaśikha).
The mind the first knower assumed in order to teach (saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.25).
A topic of the Tattvasamāsa (17); in the Kramadīpikā, Brahmā's creation, from the subtle elements, of provision for the beings he had produced.
The fourteenfold creation of beings: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53; Tattvasamāsa 18).
Resolve, self-assertion, desire, the task of awareness, and action — the functions of buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the two sets of capacities (Tattvasamāsa 8; Kramadīpikā).
Five sources of action — steadfastness, faith, seeking happiness, the wish not to know, the wish to know — of which only the wish to know leads to liberation (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 9).
Five agents: vaikārika (good acts), taijasa (bad), bhūtādi (deluded), sānumāna (good-deluded), niranumāna (bad-deluded) (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 11).

The Sāṃkhya Sūtra's account of error: what appears in error is both existent and non-existent, since it is sublated (as there) and not sublated (as real elsewhere) (SS 5.56), rejecting the rival accounts (5.52–55).
